nameStory: The crimped gill gets its name from its distinctive wavy, crimped appearance that looks like fabric that's been pleated or folded. The scientific name 'Plicatura' comes from the Latin word 'plicatus' meaning 'folded' or 'pleated,' perfectly describing those characteristic wrinkled surfaces that make this fungus so recognizable.
description: The crimped gill is a unique bracket-like fungus that forms thin, shelf-like growths on dead hardwood trees. Rather than typical gills or pores, it has a wrinkled, folded underside that looks like someone crimped paper or fabric. These overlapping, fan-shaped brackets are usually small, rarely exceeding a few inches across, and have a leathery texture when fresh. It's a saprophyte, meaning it feeds on dead wood and helps decompose fallen logs and dying trees.

idTips.label: Underside
idTips.description: The defining feature - deeply wrinkled, folded surfaces instead of regular gills or pores, looking like crimped fabric with wavy ridges and valleys

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms overlapping, fan-shaped or bracket-like shelves that emerge sideways from dead wood, often in clusters

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Leathery and flexible when fresh, becoming papery and brittle when dry, with a smooth upper surface

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Upper surface is pale brown to grayish-brown, while the crimped underside is typically cream to pale yellow

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Always found on dead hardwood, especially favoring beech, alder, and hazel trees and their fallen branches

habitat: Look for crimped gill on dead hardwood trees throughout New England's mixed forests, particularly on beech, alder, and hazel. It's most common on fallen logs, dead branches still attached to trees, and stumps in moist woodland areas. You'll often find it in deciduous or mixed forests where these host trees are present, from lowland areas up to moderate elevations.

seasonality.spring: Fresh growth begins as weather warms and moisture increases. New brackets appear pale and flexible, with the crimped undersides most pronounced.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season when brackets are most visible and well-developed. Look after rain when the leathery texture is most apparent.
seasonality.fall: Mature brackets become more papery and brittle. Still easily identifiable by the characteristic crimped undersides even as they begin to fade.
seasonality.winter: Persistent year-round, though older brackets may become weathered and brittle. The folded structure remains visible even on dried specimens.

funFact: This fungus is experiencing a mysterious population boom in Britain, with nearly 80% of all recorded sightings happening since the year 2000, often appearing in areas where it had never been seen before - scientists aren't sure if it's actually spreading or if people are just getting better at noticing its unique crimped features!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other small bracket fungi, but the deeply crimped, folded underside is unique - no other common bracket fungus has this pleated appearance instead of regular pores or smooth surfaces. Remember: if it looks like someone crimped the underside with a fork, it's probably this species.
contextualKnowledge: There's some taxonomic confusion with this species - you may see it listed as Plicaturopsis crispa in some older field guides, but it's now classified in the genus Plicatura. Both names refer to the same distinctive crimped fungus, so don't be confused by the different scientific names in various sources.
compareHints: Crimped gill differs from its relative the snow-white crust (Plicatura nivea) by its bracket-like growth form and distinct folded underside - the snow-white crust forms flat, smooth, white patches directly on wood surfaces without the characteristic crimping. While both are saprophytes on dead wood, only crimped gill has that unmistakable pleated texture that makes it look like nature's origami.
